strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful efficiency bottleneck: visual tokens substantially increase the language model’s input length. Applying selection and merging before the projector is a simple, practically relevant design.
PruMerge+ demonstrates a useful accuracy–compression tradeoff. With 25% of image tokens, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2 and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench (Table 1).

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. Training-free Video-LLaVA results are encouraging, including an ActivityNet-QA improvement from 45.3 to 48.3 with PruMerge (Table 3).

The ablations provide evidence that informed selection and merging help: training-free TextVQA accuracy exceeds spatial sampling in Table 4, and adding token supplementation improves results in Table 5. Core models, image datasets, and related methods are cited, and a project page is linked.
weaknesses: The central practical efficiency claim lacks measured validation. Table 2 reports roofline estimates for LLM prefill, without measured end-to-end latency, decoding throughput, or pruning/merging overhead. It also analyzes aggressive PruMerge compression rather than the PruMerge+ configuration providing the strongest accuracy tradeoff. Consequently, the deployment benefit at the preferred operating point remains uncertain.

The algorithm does not consistently specify the reported token budgets. Algorithm 1 adds m spatial samples to m selected anchors, which would increase the reported 5.5% retention to approximately 11%, whereas Table 1 reports 25% for PruMerge+. Its subsequent loop and output still reference only m tokens. The neighbor count k, attention-head aggregation, and normalization of merging weights are also unspecified. These ambiguities affect reproduction of the main results.

The comparison protocol is insufficiently controlled or documented. Table 7 does not establish whether ToMe, ATS, and EViT receive the same LoRA fine-tuning as PruMerge+, or explain their reduction schedules and insertion layers. CrossGet results are imported from its paper. Matching token ratios alone does not establish that the performance differences arise from the proposed algorithm.

The claimed O(n) clustering complexity in Section 2.2 is unsupported by the described computation. Comparing m anchors against n tokens requires O(mn) similarities, ignoring feature dimension; with a fixed retained fraction, this scales quadratically. Section 3.3 additionally describes the full KK-transpose matrix. This undermines the asserted asymptotic advantage over CrossGet.

The performance-preservation claims overstate the aggressive variant’s results. For 7B PruMerge, VQAv2 falls from 78.5 to 72.0, POPE from 85.9 to 76.3, and MME from 1510.7 to 1350.3 (Table 1). Section 4.1 also claims improved POPE performance despite the reported decreases. The claims should clearly distinguish aggressive compression from the more accurate PruMerge+ setting.

The distinctive contribution of adaptive IQR selection is not adequately isolated. The method combines established attention-based selection, outlier detection, and similarity-based merging, but lacks a fixed top-k attention baseline at matched average budgets. A few visualizations and benchmark-average token counts do not establish that the adaptive rule reliably allocates tokens according to image complexity or preserves question-relevant details.
